Here's a brief summary of the history of Great Zimbabwe ruins:

Great Zimbabwe was an ancient city located in southern Africa. The first settlers arrived around 1000 AD, with construction beginning on the site around 1100 AD and continuing until about 1500 AD. It served as the capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe from the early 13th century onward, and was abandoned sometime in the 16th or 17th centuries.

The Stone Structure at Great Zimbabwe is considered one of the largest in precolonial Southern Africa. The site spans an area of 2.79 square miles, with its peak population estimated to have been around 20,000 people between the early 13th and late 15th centuries. Archaeological and historical evidence suggests that the actual population of the city did not exceed 10,000 people.

The Zimbabwean state was centered on it, covering an area of approximately 98,400 square miles (256,000 km²). This makes Great Zimbabwe one of the largest cities in precolonial Africa. UNESCO recognized the site as a World Heritage Site in 1986.

The Great Zimbabwe ruins are now located in modern-day Zimbabwe and neighboring countries.

Here is a brief summary of the history of Hagia Sophia:

Hagia Sophia, officially known as the Hagia Sophia Grand Mosque, is an important historical site located in Istanbul, Turkey. The building began its existence as a church from 360 CE and continued to serve that purpose until it was converted into a museum starting in 1935.

After years of being a mosque, it reverted back to serving as one on February 24, 2020. Prior to this, the site had been transformed by various rulers throughout history: in 1204–1261, it was occupied and partially destroyed by Crusaders during the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem; then after the Fall of Constantinople in 1453, it served as a mosque before being made into a museum again. 

The current structure is believed to have been built by Emperor Justinian I starting from 532-537 CE and was designed by Greek geometers Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles.

Hagia Sophia has played significant roles in various historical periods, including serving as a cathedral for the Byzantine liturgical tradition until its fall to Constantinople, then being used as a mosque during the Crusades. The building's architecture is considered an example of Byzantine style, and it underwent numerous changes over time before finally becoming a museum on February 24, 2020.

The Trans-Amazonian Highway, also known as BR-230 in Portuguese pronunciation: [ho.doˈvi.ɐ tɾɐ̃.za.maˈzõ.ni.kɐ], was introduced on September 27, 1972 and is the third longest highway in Brazil at a length of 4,000 kilometers. It runs through Amazon forest regions and states such as Paraíba, Ceará, Piauí, Maranhão, Tocantins, Pará, and Amazonas, stretching from the proximity of Saboeiro to Lábrea.

The project was initiated by the military dictatorship ruling Brazil from 1964 to 1985, primarily for controlling the remote regions and promoting economic engagement with the region's natural resources. The highway was designed to connect these areas with other parts of the country as well as neighboring countries such as Colombia, Peru, and Ecuador.

Originally planned to be a fully paved highway 5,200 kilometers long, modifications were made after its inauguration due to budget constraints and other factors. This historical project aimed to provide access for settlement in largely unpopulated regions, alleviating the effects of droughts on land that could have been settled elsewhere.

Seismographs became widely adopted following the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, which caused widespread devastation in Europe.
